concepts.bodyMd:
*   **Telangana** has one of the earliest histories in India, sitting at the meeting point of northern and southern kingdoms.
*   The name "Telangana" itself is comparatively recent — it came into use only from the time of the **Delhi Sultans**, first mentioned by the poet **Amir Khusrau**. At that point it referred to a much wider Telugu-speaking belt, sometimes stretching all the way to Tamil Nadu.
*   Under **Golconda Qutub Shahi** rule, "Telangana" also covered Coastal Andhra. It was only later, once the **Nizam** handed Northern Circars (Coastal Andhra) and Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema) to the East India Company, that "Telangana" narrowed down to specifically mean the Telugu-speaking parts of **Hyderabad State**.
*   Telugu speakers have historically been called **Andhras**, their land **Andhra Desa**. The **Buddhist Jatakas (600–400 B.C.E.)** already refer to the land between the Godavari and Krishna rivers as **Andhapatham/Andhakaratham**.
*   Before the Satavahanas, the region was made up entirely of **republics (gana rajyas)** — one of these was ruled by a king named **Shalivahanudu**.

### Earliest References

*   The **earliest reference to the Andhras** appears in the **Aitareya Brahmana of the Rigveda (1000 B.C.E.)**: sage Vishwamitra curses his fifty sons to live south of the Vindhyas among the Andhra, Pundra, Pulinda, Sabara and Mutiba tribes — all described as non-Aryan stock.
*   **Sage Agastya** is credited (in the Puranas, Mahabharata, and Sangam literature) with bringing Aryan culture into the south — the Mahabharata even has him crushing Vindhya's pride and drinking the ocean dry, symbolizing this southward push.
*   Among the 16 Mahajanapadas of the 6th century B.C.E., **Asmaka** (Nizamabad, Karimnagar, Adilabad districts) was the only one located in South India, with its capital at **Podana** (present-day Bodhan). The kingdoms of **Alaka (Asmaka)** and **Mulaka** (Nanded, Aurangabad districts) lay on either side of the Godavari and were together known as "**Andhakarattas**"; Mulaka's capital was **Prathistanapura (Paithan)**.
*   **Megasthenes**, the Greek ambassador who visited India in the 4th century B.C.E., recorded that the Andhras commanded **30 fortified cities, 1 lakh infantry, 2,000 cavalry, and 1,000 elephants** — a claim **Pliny** later confirmed. The forts he described have been identified at Bodhan, Kotilingala, Dhulikatta, Peddabankur, Kondapur, Phanigiri, Gajulabanda, Indrapuri (Telangana) and Sathanikota, Veerapuram, Bhattiprolu, Dhanyakatakam, Vijayapuri, Suvarnagiri, Vengi, Narasala (Andhra Pradesh).
*   Ashoka's **13th Rock Edict** places the kingdoms of Kalinga, Andhra, Bojaka and Rattika just south of his empire, following his dharma.
*   After Mauryan power collapsed, **Pushyamitra Sunga** — commander-in-chief — killed the last Mauryan emperor **Brihadradha** and seized the throne in **187 B.C.E.**; the Andhras rose in rebellion against this but were defeated by the Sungas (recorded in Kalidasa's _Malavikagnimitra_).

### Pre-Satavahana Petty Kingdoms (2nd–1st century B.C.E.)

*   With the Mauryas gone and the Satavahanas yet to rise, the Deccan was ruled by scattered local kings.
*   The **Datukaranda inscriptions** (Bhattiprolu Stupa, 3rd century B.C.E.) name a king **Kubiraka**, who ruled with the help of a Nigamasabha and Gostis. The **Vaddemanu inscriptions** add names like Rajasomaka, Guntupalli, Velpuru, and Sarisada, Mahasada, Ashokasada, Shivasada, Shivamahasada.
*   Coins from this era — of Maharathi and Mahatalavara rulers (Kondapur, Hyderabad, Kotilingala) and of Gobada, Samagopa, Narana, Kamvayasiri (Kotilingala) — along with Sivamahastin and Sivaskandahastin coins at Veerapuram, fill out the picture of these small kingdoms.
*   Excavated pre-Satavahana habitations at Kondapur, Peddabankur and Kotilingala show red and red-black pottery, and evidence that iron was already being melted and worked into plough rods and tools — a blacksmith's furnace has been found at **Peddabankur** (Karimnagar district).

* * *

*   Reconstructing Satavahana history relies on two kinds of evidence: **literary sources** and **archaeological sources** (inscriptions, coins, monuments, paintings, sculpture).

### Inscriptions

*   All known Satavahana inscriptions are in **Prakrit, written in Brahmi script**, and only **24** survive from the dynasty's entire long rule — 8 from Nasik, 5 from Kanheri, 3 from Karle, 1 from Bilsa, 2 from Naneghat, 1 from Mykadoni (Kurnool district), 1 from Chinaganjam, 2 from Amaravati, 1 from Kodavali. These **24 inscriptions** cover only the early and end rulers of the dynasty — no inscriptions have been found for any of the rulers who reigned in between.
*   The **Naneghat inscription**, issued by **Naganika** (wife of Satakarni I), is a decorative record carved with figures of the early Satavahanas. 
*   The **Kanheri inscription** was issued by **Krishna (Kanha)**. 
*   The **Nasik inscription of Gautami Balasri** — issued in the 19th regnal year of her grandson Vashistiputra Sri Pulomavi — recounts the conquests of her son **Gautamiputra Satakarni**. And the **Hathigumpha inscription** of the Kalinga king **Kharavela** (Maha Meghavahana dynasty), though not a Satavahana record itself, is one of the most valuable sources for Satavahana chronology, since it describes his contemporary, Satakarni.

### Coins

*   The Satavahanas minted mostly **lead and copper** coins, along with **Potin** coins (an alloy of copper, tin and other metals); **silver coins** appear only from the time of **Gautamiputra Satakarni** onward. Coins typically carried the king's name and titles, sometimes the father's name too, and were deciphered through epigraphic script analysis. Common symbols include the **ox, elephant, lion, hill, Ujjain symbol, ship, sun, moon, lotus and couch**.
*   The single strongest piece of evidence for the dynasty's Telangana origins comes from coinage: coins of **Chimuka Satavahana** and **Satakarni I** are found at Kotilingala, and since **Chimuka's coins turn up in greatest numbers only at Kotilingala**, this points to Telangana as the Satavahanas' first home. Many of these ruler names — previously known only from Puranas or scattered inscriptions — came to light after **Sanganabatla Narahari Sarma**, a Postal Department employee, collected Kotilingala coins and handed them to epigraphist **Dr. P.V. Parabrahma Sastry** in 1970.
*   Coins also surface at Nevasa, Maski (Karnataka), Tripuri (Madhya Pradesh), Nagarjunakonda, Kondapur and Peddabankur. A distinctive category, **restruck coins** — where one ruler's symbols are stamped over another's — arises between contemporaries, through inheritance, rebellion, or conquest. 
*   The most famous example: **9,270 silver coins** of the Western Kshatrapa ruler **Nahapana**, found at Tarahala and Jogalthembi, restruck by **Gautamiputra Satakarni** — direct numismatic proof of his victory over Nahapana. 
*   Coins of **Rudrasena II** found at the Buddhist site of **Phanigiri** (Nalgonda district) point to ongoing Satavahana–Kshatrapa contact, while a **ship-figure coin of Yagnasri Satakarni** at Nagarjunakonda is evidence of sea trade. 
*   Higher officials — Mahatalavara, Mahasenapati, Maharathi, Mahagramika — also had the right to mint their own coins, as Maharathi **Sadakana (Satakarni) Kalalaya** did. **Roman coins**, found at several South Indian sites, arrived through India's trade relations with Rome.

### Excavations & Monuments

*   Chronology at these sites has largely been fixed through **carbon dating**. Key Telangana excavation sites include **Phanigiri, Gajulabanda, Kotilingala, Peddabankur, Kadambapur, Dhulikatta**; in Andhra, Amaravati, Bhattiprolu, Gudivada, Jaggayyapeta, Guntupalli, Ramateertham and Salihundam.

#### Kondapur

*   Located in **Medak district**, Kondapur was already a town by the 3rd century B.C.E. and, before the Satavahanas, served as the capital of the **Asika kingdom** (Rangareddy, Hyderabad, Medak districts) — one of the 30 forts Megasthenes described. 
*   It functioned as a major Roman trade hub; a necklace of Roman sestertii bearing the **Tiberius Caesar** symbol has been found here, along with **4,000 Satavahana coins** naming rulers such as Sadavahana, Gauthamiputra Satakarni, Vasishtiputra Satakarni, Vasishtiputra Pulumavi, Shivasri Pulumavi III and Yagnasri Satakarni. **Mallampalli Somasekhara Sarma** believed Kondapur served as the Satavahanas' **mint center**.

#### Kotilingala

*   Sitting at the confluence of the Peddavagu and Godavari in Karimnagar district, Kotilingala was excavated between 1980–1983, uncovering the walls of a Satavahana **fort and town**, along with coins of **Simuka** and pre-Satavahana rulers. 
*   This site was already prominent by the 4th century B.C.E., and everything points to it being the **first capital of the Satavahana Empire** — a sandstone pillar found here bears "**Naga gopi nikaya**" in Brahmi script. Nearby, at **Munula Gutta**, Jain stone shades have also been found.

#### Peddabankur

*   On the bank of the Hussaimiya rivulet in Karimnagar district, a farmer's field turned up a pot holding over **22,000 Satavahana coins**. Excavations between 1968–74 revealed three brick forts, 22 hand-dug wells (brick-lined), and one well built from earthen bangles, along with iron axes, pins, swords, spears, sickles, chisels, beads, bangles and terracotta seals. Coins of Satavahana, Satakarni, Pulumavi and Sivasri Pulumavi turned up alongside **Roman coins of Augustus Caesar and Tiberius**.

#### Dhulikatta

*   Dhulikatta, also on the Hussaimiya rivulet in Karimnagar district, was excavated between 1972–75 by archaeologist **V.V. Krishna Sastry**, bringing to light a Satavahana-period Buddhist Stupa with Brahmi inscriptions on the surrounding stone slabs. 
*   The name "Dhulikatta" itself means "mud fort" — inside it, palaces, walls, granaries and circular fortifications have been found, along with iron weapons, terracotta dolls, an ivory comb made from elephant tusk, earthen pots, and even Mauryan-era punch-marked coins. 
*   Buddhist monuments of this kind broadly fall into Stupas, Chaityas and Sangharamas; the sculptural style associated with the period is known as Amaravati sculpture, and it remains our best window into contemporary dress, hairstyle and jewellery.

### Literary Sources

*   The **Puranas** (Vishnu, Bhagavata, Matsya, and the _Kaliyuga Rajavrithantam_ portion of the Bhavishya Purana) preserve dynastic genealogies, but since they were compiled centuries after Satavahana rule ended, **inscriptions and coins remain the more reliable sources** — of the 30 rulers the Puranas list, almost nothing is known about rulers from 4 to 22. **Pargitar** translated these Puranic king-lists into English as _Dynasties of the Kali Age_.
*   Works like the **Gathasaptasati**, **Brihatkatha**, and **Lilavati** — all associated with the time of **Hala** — and Vatsayana's **Kamasutra** shed light on administration and everyday social life.
*   Among foreign sources, Megasthenes' _Indica_ (4th century B.C.E.), the Roman historian **Pliny's** (28–79 C.E.) _Historia Naturalis_, and the anonymous sailor's account _Periplus of the Erythrean Sea_ (~60 C.E.) together describe India's eastern trade, ports and commercial towns during Satavahana times.

* * *

concepts.partName: The Original Home of the Satavahanas — Historians' Debate
concepts.bodyMd:
_(A genuine, unresolved dispute among historians.)_

**1\. Coastal Andhra Argument** — R.G. Bhandarkar, V.A. Smith, Barnet and J. Rapson placed the homeland between the Godavari and Krishna rivers, with **Dhanyakatakam (Amaravati)** as the first capital.

*   V.A. Smith and Dr. Burgess instead favoured **Srikakulam** as the first capital.
*   D.R. Bhandarkar argued for **"Andhranagari"** on the river Telivaha.
*   Gurti Venkat Rao held that the dynasty was born in Coastal Andhra and spread east to west, with the capital shifting to Dhanyakatakam only later.

**2\. Maharashtra Argument** — P.T. Srinivasa Ayangar, K. Gopalachary, D.C. Sircar and Bhandary argued for Maharashtra instead, with **Prathishtanapuram (Paithan)** as the first capital, holding that Vashistiputra Pulumavi was the one who conquered Andhra Desa. Their case rests on four points:

*   The earliest inscriptions are found only at Naneghat and Nasik.
*   Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription records his invasion of Satakarni's kingdom.
*   Gautami Balasri's Nasik inscription doesn't mention Andhra areas within Gautamiputra's empire.
*   The Amaravati inscription — issued by Vashistiputra Pulumavi — is the first Satavahana record found in Andhra at all, with none of the earlier rulers represented there.

**3\. Vidarbha Argument** — V.V. Mirasi proposed Vidarbha instead, arguing the Satavahanas were "Andhrabhrityas" rather than Andhras proper.

*   He pointed to Gautamiputra Satakarni calling himself "benakatasami" in a Nasik inscription, identifying "Katakam on the Bena river" with the Kanhan (a Wainganga tributary) as the likely capital.
*   This view found little support beyond suggesting Vidarbha was simply one part of the empire under Satakarni I and Gautamiputra.

**4\. Karnataka Argument** — Dr. V.S. Suktankar argued for Ballari (Karnataka).

*   He cited the Mykadoni inscription of Pulumavi (the last Satavahana ruler, found in Kurnool district, referring to a place called "Satavahanahara") and the Hirahadagalli copper-plate inscription of the Pallava king Shivaskanda Varma IV (referring to "Satavahana Ratta").
*   Suktankar was also the first to propose that the Satavahanas were a sub-dynasty among the Andhras, and that "Andhra" (of the Puranas) and "Satavahana" (of the inscriptions) referred to two different ruling groups — Andhras in the Andhra region, Satavahanas in Maharashtra.

**5\. Telangana Argument** — Ajaymitra Sastry, Deme Raji Reddy, Thakur Rajaram Singh, Krishna Sastry and archaeologist P.V. Parabrahma Sastry built their case on coin distribution.

*   Chimuka Satavahana and Satakarni coins turn up at Kotilingala, Peddabankur, Dhulikatta, Kadambapur and Kondapur — all in Telangana.
*   Since Srimuka's coins are found only at Kotilingala, he must have founded the dynasty there, making Kotilingala the first capital.
*   Kharavela's claim (in the Hathigumpha inscription) of invading the Satavahana kingdom from the west lends further support.
*   On the whole, the coin and inscription evidence points fairly clearly to the Satavahanas establishing their kingdom at Kotilingala and extending first into southern Maharashtra — though nothing confirms it reached Coastal Andhra first from Telangana.

### Are the Satavahanas and the Andhras One?

**1.** E.J. Rapson, R.G. Bhandarkar, L.D. Barnett, Maramanda Rama Rao hold that the Satavahanas of the inscriptions and the Andhras of the Puranas are simply the same people under two names: "Andhra" denoting nationality, "Satavahana" the ruling family.

*   The genealogies in the Matsya and Vayu Puranas line up with those in the inscriptions.
*   The dynasty went by several names in different sources — Salivahanas, Satakarnis, Andhras, Andhrabhrityas.
*   Hala himself used Salivahana, Satavahana and Satakarni interchangeably in the Gathasaptasati.
*   The grammarian Hemachandra considered "Salivahana" simply a corrupted form of "Satavahana."
*   The Jain writer Jinaprabha Suri offered a folk etymology: the name arose because "hundreds of vehicles" (satavahana) were donated by the dynasty's founder.

**2.** H.C. Roychowdary and Srinivas Sastry, building on P.V. Parabrahma Sastry's Telangana-origin theory, read the evidence differently.

*   Under Samagopa, who ruled from Kotilingala, a commander named Sirisatavahana served him before declaring independence — which is why the Puranas remember the dynasty as "Andhrabhrityas," former servants of the Andhras.
*   This camp also points out that the Satavahanas used Prakrit while Telugu was the Andhras' language, treating this as evidence the two were genuinely distinct peoples.

**3.** A traditional story, recorded in the Kathasaritsagaram (based on Gunadhya's Brihatkatha), explains where the name "Satavahana" came from — not a historical argument like points 1 and 2, but a passed-down tale.

*   A Yaksha (semi-divine being) named Sata existed, in the shape of a lion.
*   King Deepakarni killed this lion-shaped Yaksha.
*   Inside it, a boy was found, whom Deepakarni raised as his own.
*   Because the boy was discovered inside the Yaksha "Sata," he was named Satavahana — the story behind the dynasty's name.

* * *

*   Satavahana chronology is a genuinely difficult problem. Historians disagree sharply on when the dynasty **began**, though there's broad agreement it **ended around 225–230 C.E.**
*   The Puranic accounts themselves conflict: 

*   The **Matsya Purana** lists 30 Andhra kings ruling 456 years, while the **Vayu Purana** counts only 17 kings over 272 years — and several named rulers have no surviving inscriptions or coins to confirm them.
*   Working from **Pargitar's** Puranic king-list, scholars like V.V. Mirasi, Dr. K. Gopalachary, Gurti Venkat Rao and Maramanda Rama Rao support a **"long chronology"** of roughly 450 years, running from 220 B.C.E. to 225 C.E. — Gurti Venkat Rao ties this to the succession war after Bindusara's death in 271 B.C.E., during which **Simuka** seized the opportunity to declare independence.

* * *

*   Scholars disagree on the Satavahanas' caste — the evidence points in several different directions.
*   The **Brahmin case**: Gautamiputra Satakarni is called "**Eka Brahmana**" (unparalleled Brahmin), "Kshatriya Darpamana Mardana" and "Dvijavara Kutumba Vivardhana" in the Nasik inscription, and Satavahana kings took their **mother's gotra**, which some read as an official declaration of Brahmin descent.
*   **Kshatriya case**: Governance was seen as a Kshatriya's duty. Gautami Balasri is called "Rajarshi Vadhuvu" and "Kshatriya Patni" in her Nasik inscription, and the dynasty performed **Asvamedha and Rajasuya** sacrifices — rites traditionally reserved for Kshatriyas.
*   A **Naga-race theory** draws on the _Dvatrimsat Puttalika_, which claims the dynasty's founder was born to a Naga king of the Godavari coast and a Brahmin woman.
*   **Sudra**: The _Bhagavata Purana_ calls Simuka "**Vrishaludu**," implying mixed parentage; in Kannada, "Satavahana" means "**ryot**" (farmer) — taken as pointing to Sudra origins.

* * *

Historians split the dynasty into **Early Satavahanas** (from the founding up to Gautamiputra Satakarni's accession) and **Later Satavahanas** (from Gautamiputra Satakarni to the last king).

### Early Satavahanas

**Simuka**

*   Coins bearing the names "Sadavahana," "Satavahana" and "Chimuka" have surfaced at Kondapur, Kotilingala, near Warangal, Aurangabad, Junnar and Nevasa. Based on the script on these coins, Ajayamitra Sastry and Dr. Deme Raji Reddy identify Sadavahana with Srimuka, and hold that **Simuka was the only ruler who actually bore the name "Satavahana."**
*   The Puranas describe **Srimuka**, of the Andhra race, killing **Susarma** of the Kanva dynasty, ending Sunga authority, and founding the kingdom (they also name Sindhaka, Balapuchchaka and Bali). His coins are found only at **Kotilingala** — clearly his capital — and appear under three names: "Srichimuka," "Sirisatavahana" and "Siri Chimuka Satavahana." The Naneghat inscription records him as "Raya Simuka Satavahana Sirimato."
*   Jain accounts say he embraced Jainism and built several temples, and that he ruled **23 years**; but they also describe him turning cruel and anti-people in his final years, leading to his deposition and murder — a portrayal likely coloured by the fact that Simuka reverted to Vedic dharma toward the end of his reign.

**Krishna (Kanha)**

*   Simuka's brother and successor; the Puranas credit him with an **18-year** reign. He was the **first Satavahana ruler to issue an inscription** — his Nasik record mentions a Mahamatra constructing a cave for Buddhist monks, still using Mauryan administrative terminology. Under him the kingdom's western boundary extended as far as **Nasik**.

**Satakarni I**

*   Third in the Puranic list and son of Srimuka, Satakarni I ruled **18 years** and is the ruler named in the Naneghat inscription. His wife **Nayanika (Naganika)**, daughter of Maharathi Tranakayiro, is shown there alongside their sons — **Kumara Hakusri Sati Srimat**, **Kumara Satavahana**, and the elder son **Vedisri**. After Satakarni's death, Naganika ran the administration herself until Vedisri came of age. Satakarni performed **two Asvamedha sacrifices and one Rajasuya**, plus 20 other rites, donating thousands of Karshapanas along with cows, elephants and horses — earning him the titles "Apratihata Chakra," "Veera," "Sura" and "Dakshinapathipati" from Naganika.
*   The Hathigumpha inscription records that Kharavela, in his second regnal year, sent his army west — "not caring for Satakarni" — reaching the Kanna-Bena river and attacking Mushika Nagaram. Dr. R. Subrahmanyam identifies Mushika Nagaram with Kondapur, though the _Chulla Kalinga Jatakam_ instead credits Asmaka king Aruna with conquering Kalinga. 
*   The Matsya Purana lists a further **18 kings** between Satakarni I and Gautamiputra Satakarni (whom it numbers as the 23rd king), but not one of them is confirmed by an inscription or coin.

**Satakarni II**

*   The sixth ruler in the Puranic list, credited with a **56-year** reign. Some scholars attribute the Sanchi Stupa inscription to him, and he is said to have taken **Malwa** from the Sakas.

**The rulers after Satakarni II**

*   Eight kings followed in succession — Lambodara, Apeelaka, Meghaswati, Swati, Skanda Swati, Mrigendra Swatikarni, Kuntala Satakarni and Swati Karni. A large copper coin found in Chanda district is thought to belong to **Apeelaka**, the eighth of these, who ruled **12 years**. During the reign of **Pulumavi I**, raids by the **Sakas and Pahlavas** in the northwest created serious instability, and efforts to bring his authority to an end failed. After his death, **Saka king Nahapana** attacked, occupied part of Maharashtra, and took the title **Mahakshatrapa**, defeating **Sundara Satakarni, Chakora Satakarni and Sivaswati** in the process.

**Hala**

*   The **17th king** of the dynasty, and a genuine literary figure in his own right — earning the title "**Kavivatsala**" and composing the **Gathasaptasati (Sattasayi)**, according to Bana's _Harsha Charitra_. He married the Simhala princess **Lilavati**, a union the _Lilavati Kavya_ (by Kutuhala) places at Saptama Godavari before the god Bheemeshwara — a site **Dr. Sanganabhatla Narsaiah** identifies as present-day Vempalli Venkatrao pet in Karimnagar district.

### Later Satavahanas

**Gautamiputra Satakarni (106–130 C.E.)**

You're right — the sub-heading treatment for Gautamiputra makes the plain paragraphs for the other rulers stick out and feel inconsistent. Here's the full "Later Satavahanas" section with matching sub-bullet breakdowns for all of them:

### Gautamiputra Satakarni (106–130 C.E.)

*   Widely regarded as the **greatest** of all Satavahana rulers, and 23rd in the Puranic list, he ruled effectively for **24 years**. Everything known about his conquests comes from a single source: the **Nasik inscription** his mother **Gautami Balasri** issued after his death, in the 18th regnal year of his son Vasishtiputra Pulumavi.

**Conquests and empire**

*   Defeated the **Sakas, Yavanas and Pallavas**, and **uprooted the Kshatrapa dynasty**.
*   Conquered **Anupa, Aparanta, Saurashtra, Kukura and Avanti**.
*   Empire stretched across: Asika (Hyderabad, Medak), Asmika (Nizamabad, Aurangabad), Mulaka (Paithan area), Aparanta (Bombay, Konkan, Puna), Anoopa (upper Mahishmati), Vidarbha (Nagapur, Berar), Akara (Vidisa, eastern Malwa), Avanti (Ujjain, western Malwa), Saurashtra (South Kathiawad) and Kukura (South Rajasthan).

**Titles**

*   Titled "lord of the mountain regions" — Vindhya, Achavata, Pariyata, Vahya, Kanvagiri, Siritana, Malaya, Mahendra, Sita, Chekora.
*   The Nasik inscription adds further epithets: "Satavahanakula Yasah Pratistapana Kara," "Kshatriya Darpamana Mardana," "Ksharahata Vamsa Niravasheshakara," "Saka, Yavana, Pahlava Nishudana," "Eka Brahmana," "Eka Sura," "Eka Dhanurdhana," "Agama Nilaya," and "Trisamudratoyapitavahana" — one whose horses drank the water of three seas.

**Evidence**

*   Victory over Nahapana confirmed materially: **9,270** of Nahapana's silver coins, restruck by Gautamiputra, found at **Jogalthembi**.
*   Issued two inscriptions in the Nasik caves, in his **18th and 24th** regnal years.
*   Coins turn up in the hundreds at **Kondapur and Peddabankur**.

### Vashishtiputra Pulumavi (Pulumavi II, 130–154 C.E.)

*   Inscriptions spread across **Nasik, Karle, Amaravati, Myakadoni and Banavasi**.
*   Ruled from **Dhanyakatakam**.
*   Called "**Dakshinapatiswara**" in Gautami Balasri's Nasik inscription.

### Vashishtiputra Satakarni (154–165 C.E.)

*   The Kshatrapa **Rudradaman**, in his **Junagadh inscription**, claims to have twice defeated a "Satakarni, lord of Dakshinapatha" — very likely this ruler.
*   His silver and lead coins turn up across the Godavari and Krishna regions.
*   Mentioned in a **Kanheri inscription** issued by his queen, who identifies herself as the daughter of Mahakshatrapa Rudradaman.
*   By this point — or by the time of his predecessor Vashishtiputra Pulumavi — the Satavahanas appear to have already lost their Maharashtrian territory to the Kshatrapas.

### Yagnasri Satakarni (165–194 C.E.)

*   The **last great Satavahana ruler**, 26th in the Puranic list, with a reign the Puranas put at **29 years**.
*   Inscriptions: two survive at **Kanheri**, with others at **Nasik and Chinaganjam** (Krishna district).
*   Coins bearing a **ship with two sails** attest to continued maritime activity.
*   Patronized **Acharya Nagarjuna** and Buddhism; praised as "**Trisamudradhiswara**" in Bana's _Harsha Charitra_.
*   The _Katha Saritsagara_ records that Nagarjuna was killed by the Satavahana crown prince — plunging the kingdom into chaos.
*   Yagnasri was ultimately **defeated by Rudradaman**, losing the western part of the empire.

### Decline

*   After Yagnasri, three kings — **Vijaya Satakarni, Chandasri and Pulumavi IV** — ruled a combined **17 years**.
*   **Pulumavi IV** was the last of the line (a Myakadoni inscription of his, from Kurnool district, survives).
*   The empire unravelled after him, as the **Abhiras, Ikshavakus, Chutus and Pallavas** broke away, establishing their own independent kingdoms and bringing the Satavahana age to a close.

* * *

The Satavahanas began by **following Mauryan administrative traditions**, and in turn became the model later dynasties copied. Most of what is known comes from the **Nasik and Karle cave inscriptions**.

### Powers of the Emperor

*   The king headed the state as supreme authority and supreme commander-in-chief, ruling as a **hereditary monarch**. Some kings took their mother's name, but royal power itself remained strictly with the males, who bore titles like Raja and Maharaja. Kings performed **Asvamedha and Rajasuya** sacrifices, and over time the idea of **divine right monarchy** took hold — kings were seen as embodying the qualities of Puranic figures like Rama and Vishnu, expected to be bound by the Dharmasastras and to protect Dharma.

### Administrative Staff

*   The king was assisted by **Amatyas, Mahamatras and Visvasamatyas**, and a wider body of officials: **Maharathis** (provincial governors), **Mahabhojakas** (governor-equivalent status), **Mahasenapati** (army commander), **Bhandarika** (keeper of income-in-kind), **Heranika/Hiranyaka** (treasurer), **Dutakas** (spies), **Lekhaka** (the emperor's security), **Nibandhakara** (registered documents), **Mahataraka** (bodyguard), a second sense of **Mahamatras** (overseeing Buddhist-monk affairs), and **Gramaka** (village officials).

### Administrative Units

*   The kingdom was organized into three tiers: the **Rajakamkheta** region under the king's direct rule, the **feudatory areas**, and the **border areas**. 
*   Feudatories included the Chutus (Mysore), Kurus (Kolhapur), Ikshavakus (Vijayapuri), and the Maharathis/Mahabhojas of Maharashtra, with the crown maintaining marriage alliances with several of them; toward the end of the dynasty, border defence fell to army commanders, who gradually turned into landed feudal lords in their own right.
*   Below that, the kingdom was divided into **Aharas** (provinces) governed by Amatyas — Soparahara, Govardhanahara (Nasik), Mamalahara and Satavahana among them, often named after their capitals. Cities were run by **Nigama Sabhas**, which doubled as trade associations, with caste elders called **Gahapatis** serving as members — the Bhattiprolu inscription references one such Sabha. 
*   Major cities of the era included Kotilingala, Dhulikatta, Yeleswaram (Nalgonda) and Kondapur in Telangana; Dhanyakatakam and Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda) in Andhra Pradesh; Govardhana, Sopara and Pratistanapura (Paithan) in Maharashtra; and Brahmagiri in Karnataka.

### The Rise of Feudatory Power

*   Feudalism crept gradually into the administrative system as regional government passed into the hands of feudatory chiefs, who paid annual tribute and supplied troops in exchange for holding the semi-independent posts of **Mahabhojas and Maharathis** — many of whom became fully independent once the Satavahanas declined. 
*   **D.D. Kosambi** points to the **Myakadoni inscription** (from the 8th regnal year of Sri Pulumavi) as the earliest concrete evidence of this process: a **Mahasenapati**, in exchange for maintaining his post, was granted rights over an entire **Ahara (district)** for army upkeep, and in turn leased one village to a subordinate official. Village administration itself sat with **Gaulmukas (Gulmika)** — who were, again, army officers.

### Village Administration

*   The village was the administrative unit below the Ahara, run by a "**Gramika**" (also Gumika/Gulmika/Galmika), who sometimes oversaw several villages at once. Only army officers held this post, whose core duties were **collecting taxes** and **keeping law and order**; because the position became **hereditary**, village officers steadily accumulated political strength — a dynamic that itself fed the rise of feudalism. Villagers, meanwhile, were subject to **vetti** (forced labour) for household and field work; the _Kamasutra_ even describes the specific kinds of vetti expected of women.

* * *

### Agriculture

*   Agriculture was the dominant occupation, built around **rice, jowar, jute, gingelly and sugarcane** as the major crops, with **wheat, red gram, black gram, castor, coconut and cotton** grown alongside. Oxen, asses and he-buffaloes did the tilling; wells were the main water source, supplemented by canals and embankments, with a device called the "**Persian Wheel**" — buckets arranged in a circle and turned by animal power — used to lift water from wells and canals. Villagers cultivating wasteland (banjar) did so as **vetti**.
*   **Land and village grants**: Rulers didn't simply seize land — they bought it from the ryots first, then granted it for religious institutions, agriculture, or tree-planting.
    
    *   **Mugudasa** donated land to clothe an ascetic.
    *   **Ushavadatta** (Kshatrapa Nahapana's son-in-law) bought land for **4,000 Karshapanas** from a Brahmin named Asvabhooti, then donated it.
    *   **Gautamiputra Satakarni** was the first to grant land to Buddhist monks with full administrative and financial rights, tax-free — marking the start of land grants to Brahmins and Buddhist monks in the region.

### Land Tax & Revenue

*   Land tax formed the government's main income, generally set at **one-sixth of the crop yield** and collected as either **Rajabhoga** or **Devameya**. The Nasik inscription notes that Gautamiputra Satakarni levied taxes in line with Dharma and justice. Beyond land tax, the state also drew duties on highways, mines, ports and passages, a profession tax called **Karukara**, a government monopoly on **salt manufacture**, and income from penalties — payable in either cash or kind. **Brahmins and ascetics were exempt from all taxation.**

### Crafts

*   Cottage industries thrived on the iron ore deposits of Medak, Nizamabad, Karimnagar and Warangal. At **Peddabankur** (200 B.C.E.–200 C.E.), burnt bricks — including roof tiles — were in wide use, alongside 22 brick-lined wells and constructed drainage canals.
*   Inscriptions name **18 distinct crafts**: Kolikas (weavers), Tilapasikas (oil extractors), Kasakaras (brass workers), Kularikas (potters), Tasakaras (shining-layer creators), Kamaras (blacksmiths), Malakaras (florists), Odayantrikas (water-machine makers), Suvarnakaras (goldsmiths), Vadhakas (carpenters), Selavadhakas (stone workers), Avasenis (handicrafters), Lekhakas (writers), Charmakara (leather workers), Pesakaras (basket makers), Mithikas (stone polishers), Gadhikas (perfume makers) and Manikaras (diamond workers). 
*   Craftsmen organized themselves into **guilds**, each headed by a "**Sreshti**" — Junnar inscriptions mention the Dhannuka (grain), Kasakara and Tesakara guilds, while Nasik records the Kularika, Tilapashika and Odayantrika guilds. These guilds effectively functioned as banks, taking deposits and issuing loans: a Junnar inscription records a Buddhist depositor's income being set aside for transplantation, and a grain merchants' guild donating a seven-room cave with its own water source.
*   A **Nasik inscription of Ushavadatta** records a handloom weavers' guild at Govardhana holding two deposits:

*   **2,000 Karshapanas at 1% per month** — interest used to clothe Buddhist monks who stayed at Nasik during the rainy season (12 Karshapanas per monk).
*   **1,000 Karshapanas at 3/4% per month** — interest used for the monks' other needs.

### Trade — Internal & External

*   Merchants engaged in foreign trade were called **Sarthavahas**, themselves organized into guilds under a **Sreshti (Setti)**. Major trade centers included Pratistanapuram, Tagara, Junnar, Nasik and Vaijayanti in Maharashtra; Dhanyakatakam, Vijayapuri, Gudur (Krishna district) and Kantakasila (Ghantasala) in Andhra Pradesh; and **Kotilingala, Dhulikatta and Kondapur** in Telangana — with the **bullock cart** as the main mode of transport.
*   India–Rome trade is documented in the _Periplus of the Erythrean Sea_, Ptolemy's _Geography_, and Pliny's _Natural History_. Roman coins have surfaced at Nellore, Attirala (Kadapa), Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Vinukonda, Chebrolu, Ongole and Nandyal in Andhra Pradesh, and at Gootiparti, Akkinapalli, Yeleswaram (Nalgonda), Nustulapur, Peddabankur (Karimnagar) and Nagavarappadu (Khammam) in Telangana; gold coins turn up at **Arikamedu** (Tamil Nadu, near Pondicherry), a major Roman trading post. Pliny records that **1.25 crore dinars** flowed from Rome to India every year.
*   India's exports to Rome ranged widely: slave women, animals, ghee, gingelly oil, silk and silk cloth, cotton cloth, pepper, herbs, betel leaves, jaggery, sandalwood, teakwood, coconuts and coconut oil, garlic, tamarind, spices, steel and spun cotton, along with pearls from Sri Lanka and Indian diamonds — the _Periplus_ specifically notes bulk pepper exports from **Mujiris (Cranganore, Kerala)**. In return, India imported silver, copper, glass articles, cosmetics and intoxicants. Because the balance of trade consistently favoured India, **Roman gold flowed steadily into the country**. Trade moved through western ports — Sopar (Sopara), Kalyan (Kalyani), Bharukachham (Broach) — and eastern ones, including Kantakasela (Ghantasala), Koddura (Gudur), Mysolia (Machilipatnam) and Allosignelu (Adurru), as Ptolemy records.

* * *

The picture of Satavahana society is pieced together from the _Katha Saritsagaram_, Kutuhala's _Lilavati_, Hala's _Gathasaptasati_, Gunadhya's _Brihatkatha_, and the sculptures at Amaravati, Bhattiprolu and Nagarjunakonda.

*   The **four-fold varna system** — Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Sudras — took firm root in Telangana during this period, as Aryan cultural influence spread through the region. Brahmins studied the Vedas and Vedangas and enjoyed both respect and tax exemption; Kshatriyas learned governance and warfare; Vaishyas ran trade and business; Sudras took up agriculture. 
*   **Foreigners** — Greeks, Sakas, Pahlavas, Kushans — assimilated readily into this framework, gaining recognition as Kshatriyas and adopting Hinduism or Buddhism: Nahapana's daughter Dakshamitra, his son-in-law Ushavadatta, Chastana's son Jayadamana, and Saka Rudradaman all took Hindu names. The caste system itself was far from rigid — inter-caste marriage was recorded, most notably Hala's marriage to a Sri Lankan princess (per the _Lilavati Kavya_), Satakarni I's marriage to the daughter of Maharathi Tranakayiro, and another Satavahana ruler's marriage to the daughter of Saka Rudradaman. **Gautamiputra Satakarni**, by contrast, took a more conservative line, proudly declaring that he worked to root out varna-violation and restore the purity of the system — a striking tension with the intermarriage evident elsewhere.
*   The **joint family** was the norm — donation records routinely list every family member. Women enjoyed real respect and freedom: upper-class women carried titles reflecting their husbands' rank (Mahabhoja, Mahasenapati, Mahatalavarini), and several Satavahana rulers took their **mother's name** before their own — Gautamiputra Satakarni, Gautamiputra Yagnasri Satakarni, Vasishtiputra Pulumavi and Kausakiputra Satakarni among them. 
*   Some women went further and took on administrative roles directly: **Naganika**, Satakarni I's widow, governed as guardian to her son Vedisri, and **Gautami Balasri**'s Nasik inscription records donations she made independently. Women also invested in trading guilds in their own right.
*   **Royal women** in particular were generous **patrons of Buddhist monks.**
*   Craft-based castes were also forming during this period — Halika (agriculturist), Gadhika (perfumer), Vadhika (carpenter), Kolikas (weavers), Tilapisaka (gingelly-oil extraction), Kamara (blacksmith), Kularika (potter), Udayantrika (irrigation specialist), Dhannuka (grain merchant), Vasakara (bamboo worker).
*   What is known of dress and ornament — clay bangles, anklets, beads, earrings, shoulder and leg bands — comes largely from excavations at Kotilingala, Dhulikatta, Peddabankur, Kandambapur and Kondapur, backed up visually by the Amaravati sculptures and paintings; both men and women wore jewellery. Music, dance, and pastimes like bullock and cock competitions filled people's leisure time. 
*   **Slavery** was also present — slaves worked in wealthy households, factories, fields and businesses, and Gunadhya's _Brihatkatha_ references an active slave trade in which slaves were, by its account, treated poorly.

* * *

Vedic religion, Buddhism and Jainism all flourished side by side in the Deccan under the Satavahanas.

### Vedic Religion

*   A number of Satavahana rulers were themselves committed to Vedic practice.

*   **Satakarni I** performed extensive Vedic rites, donating thousands of Karshapanas and cows to Brahmins (as per the Naneghat inscription), and named one of his sons "**Vedasri**." **Gautamiputra Satakarni**, styled "Eka Brahmana," went further still, holding up Puranic figures like Rama, Kesava, Arjun and Bhimsen as ideals alongside traditional Sastric learning (Nasik inscription). 
*   The Naneghat inscription itself records prayers to Sankarshana, Vasudeva, Indra, the Sun and Moon, and the Dikpalakas — Vasava, Kubera, Varun, Yama.

*   Over this period, religion visibly shifted from rite-heavy **Vedic practice** toward a more devotional **Puranic Hinduism**. The recurring names Sankarshana, Vasudeva, Kesava, Govardhana, Krishna and Gopala mark the emergence of **Vaishnavism** — the _Gathasaptasati_ praises Krishna as "Madhusudhana" and "Damodara" and references the gopikas and Yasoda, with Krishna–Vasudeva worship forming the root from which Bhagavata philosophy, and later full Vaishnava faith, grew. 
*   The **Gathasaptasati** also shows worship of **Pasupati and Gouri**. By the 2nd century B.C.E., **Siva worship** had begun in earnest — the oldest and largest surviving **Sivalinga** stands at **Gudimallam** (Chittoor district).
    
    *   **Pasupata Saivism** was formally established in the 1st century C.E. by **Lakulisa Sivacharya** and spread south during Satavahana rule.
    *   **Shakti philosophy** also began during this period.

*   Broadly, **Buddhism dominated Coastal Andhra** while **Jainism took stronger hold in Telangana**.

**Traditional/legendary roots**

*   **Rishabhanatha**, the first Tirthankara, is said to have ruled Varanasi.
*   His eldest son **Bahubali** is said to have ruled Asmaka (Bodhan).
*   The tenth Tirthankara, **Seetalanatha**, is said to have been born at **Bhadrachalam (Badalapuri)**, Khammam district.

**Spread into the Deccan**

*   Linked to a 4th-century-B.C.E. famine in Magadha, which drove Jains under **Bhadrabahu** to migrate to **Shravana Belagola** for twelve years.
*   On their return, they carried Jainism into Karnataka, Andhra and Telangana.
*   **Samprati**, Ashoka's grandson, later converted to Jainism and sent Jain preachers into the Andhra region.

**Satavahana-era evidence**

*   The dynasty's founder, **Srimuka**, was himself a follower of Jainism.
*   Four stone shades for Jain monks survive at **Munulagutta**, near his capital Kotilingala — likely used for "**Sallekhana**" (ritual fasting unto death).
*   The _Kalakasuri Prabhandha_ mentions an unnamed Satavahana king patronizing a Jain monk at Pratistanapura.
*   A Kharavela inscription found at **Guntupalli** (West Godavari district) is thought by some historians to belong to a Jain cave complex.

**Key Jain thinkers**

*   **Acharya Kondakunda** (also Padmanandi) lived in the 1st century C.E. at **Konakondla** (Kurnool district), earning the name "Kondakundacharya." He authored _Samayasara, Mulacara, Panchashaktiya_ and _Pravachanasara_, and propagated the philosophy of "**Anekantavada**."
*   Other notable acharyas: **Simhanandi** and **Arhabali**.
*   The period also saw the **council of Venakatatipuri** (identified with present-day Vijayawada), where Jains made their first attempt at compiling a formal canon.

* * *

*   Founded by **Buddha** in the 6th century B.C.E., Buddhism reached Telangana and Andhra within his own lifetime.
*   Tibetan Buddhist tradition holds that Buddha visited **Amaravati** at the request of Suchendra, king of Shambala, and taught the "Kalachakramoola Tantropadesam" there — a Tantric method from the highest yoga tantra.

**Even earlier roots — before Ashoka**

*   The _Suttanipada_'s **Bavari story** tells of Bavari, living on Kavitavana island on the Godavari (in Asmaka — Karimnagar, Nizamabad, Adilabad), who sent 16 disciples to meet Buddha at Rajagriha.
*   They returned having accepted Buddhism, and Bavari himself followed.
*   Some scholars place Bavari's habitation at **Bavanakurti**, Karimnagar district.

**Councils and early spread**

*   A century after Buddha's Mahaparinirvana, the **Second Buddhist Council** at Vaisali saw young Andhra monks, led by the monk **Mahadeva**, push for changes to Sangha regulations.
*   Orthodox monks rejected this, splitting the Sangha into **Theravadins** and **Mahasanghikas**.
*   The Mahasanghika branch may well have originated at **Dhanyakatakam** itself.
*   Ashoka's 13th rock edict confirms Andhras were already following Buddhism by his time.
*   Andhra monks ("Andhakas") took part in the **Third Buddhist Council** at Pataliputra, where the "Kathavathu" debates were held.
*   By the 2nd century B.C.E., Buddhism had put down deep roots in Telangana — the stupas at **Dhulikatta and Pasegam** stand as evidence. The Pasegam stupa, per B.N. Sastry, was built by the Buddhist scholar **Chennapoosa** (the site's older name, "Chennupoosagam," derives from his name, "Poosa" meaning "Acharya").

**Patronage**

*   Satavahana **kings**, though personally Vedic, extended patronage to Buddhism; the **queens patronized it even more visibly** — Gautamiputra Satakarni, honouring his mother Gautami Balasri, donated an entire village at **Trirasmi** to Buddhist monks.
*   Ceylon's _Mahavamsa_ records **4,60,000 monks** attending a stupa ceremony at Anuradhapura, built by the Sri Lankan king **Duppigamini** (1st century B.C.E.), a contemporary of the Satavahanas.
*   Patronage extended well beyond royalty — officials, merchants, craftsmen and wealthy women competed to donate villages, land and wealth to monks; Nasik, Junnar and Kanheri inscriptions record guilds depositing funds whose interest went to monastic upkeep.
*   Given this breadth of support, it is generally argued that **merchant patronage, not royal favour, was the real engine behind Buddhism's growth** in the region.

**Monuments built**

*   Maharashtra: Bhaja, Karle, Nasik, Kanheri, Kondane, Bhedsa.
*   Andhra Pradesh: Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Bhattiprolu, Salihundam, Allur, Ghantasala, Jaggayya Peta, Guntupalli, Ramatirtham, Bojjannakonda, Gummadidurru, Gudivada, Goli.
*   Telangana: Kondapur, Phanigiri, Tirumalagiri (Nalgonda), Dhulikatta, Pasegam, Meerjampet (Karimnagar).

**Mahayana vs. Hinayana**

*   The 1st century C.E. saw **Mahayana Buddhism** emerge in Andhra, with the Mahasanghikas as its adherents — dubbed "Andhaka Sakhas" ("blind branches") by the critic Asvaghosha.
*   **Hinayana** ("small cart"): each person must reach nirvana individually; Buddha worshipped only as a symbol.
*   **Mahayana** ("big cart"): aimed to carry as many people as possible toward nirvana; treated solitary nirvana-seeking as selfish and against Buddha's own teaching; carved and worshipped actual Buddha statues.
*   Theravadin branches: **Bhadrayanis** (Nasik, Karle inscriptions); **Dharmottareeyulu** (Sopara).
*   Mahasanghika branches: **Purvasaileeyas** (Amaravati); **Aparasailiyas** (Nagarjunakonda); plus **Rajagirikulu, Mahisasakas, Siddhantikulu**.
*   In total, **18 branches** of Buddhism took shape — **9** of them in the Andhra region alone.

**Chaityakas and iconography**

*   One further Andhra branch, the **Chaityakas**, ascribed Buddha supreme qualities and laid the groundwork for idol worship.
*   They introduced symbolic milestones from Buddha's life for veneration: the lotus (birth), the horse (the Great Departure), the Bodhi Tree (enlightenment), the Dharma Chakra (first sermon), the stupa (nirvana), the trisula (the three jewels), and footprints (his continued presence).
*   Since depicting Buddha in human form had earlier been prohibited, his **footprints** were carved instead — as at the Dhulikatta stupa, alongside a small Brahmi inscription.
*   **Naga (serpent) worship** was woven into the same iconography: serpents curl around stupas in relief; a five-headed **nagamuchilinda** appears at Dhulikatta; at Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda, cobras raise their hoods over the seated Buddha, with serpent kings and queens shown in prayer.

**Acharya Nagarjuna**

*   Contemporary of Yagnasri Satakarni; remembered as a genuine polymath, often called the "second Buddha."
*   The _Lankavatara Sutram_ places his birth in Vedali village, which scholars generally locate in Telangana (near South Kosala, per the Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang).
*   Founded universities at **Nagarjunakonda and Amaravati**.
*   Developed the philosophy of "**Madhyamikavadam**," rejecting soul-philosophy and terming this position "**Sunyavadam**" (nothingness) — extended to Mahayana thought as a whole in his work _Madhyamika Karika_.
*   Chinese sources credit him with 20 works; the traveller **Itsing** (~700 C.E.) found some memorized by children and read throughout life by adults, and records his letter collection "**Suhrullekha**," addressed to Yagnasri Satakarni, was similarly memorized by children.
*   Surviving Sanskrit works: _Pragnaparamita, Ashta Sahasrika, Mula Madhyamikarikavali, Vigraha Vyaptini, Dvadaya Nikayam, Sunyasaptati_.
*   Under Mahayana influence, **Sanskrit** (rather than Prakrit) became the preferred medium for Buddhist teaching and writing.

* * *

*   The period produced a substantial body of literature in **Prakrit, Pali and Sanskrit**, with **Maharastri Prakrit** serving as the regional language and leaving a lasting imprint on Telugu itself.
*   **Hala**, the poet-king, earned the title "**Kavi Vatsala**" and compiled the **Gathasaptasati (Sattasayi)** — 700 Prakrit verses of considerable literary merit, containing numerous Telugu-origin words (Attam, Ammi, Andam, Addam, Potti, Padi among them) and beautiful depictions of rural, native life. He honoured poets **Kumarila and Sreepalita**, and women poets — **Anulakshmi, Anupalabda, Deva, Madhavi** — contributed verses of their own.
*   His minister **Gunadhya** composed the **Brihatkatha** — 7,000 slokas across seven stories — in **Paisachi**, a regional Prakrit variety. **Durnita**, of the Ganga dynasty, later translated this into Sanskrit — the moral stories of the _Panchatantram_ draw on it — and the Brihatkatha in turn inspired **Somadevasuri's** _Kathasaritsagara_ and **Kshemendra's** _Brihatkathamanjari_ in Sanskrit, while **Sarvavarma**, a contemporary of Hala, wrote the Sanskrit grammar _Katantra Vyakaranam_. **Krishna Sastry** suggests Kondapur may have been Gunadhya's home region.
*   **Vatsayana's** _Kama Sutra_, composed either in the Later Satavahana period or shortly after, treats sex and sexual life. 
*   **Kutuhala's** _Lilavati_, written in Maharashtrian Prakrit, narrates Hala's marriage to the Simhala princess before the god Bheemeswara — a site some identify with Vempalli Venkatrao pet, Karimnagar district.
*   Alongside Prakrit and Sanskrit, a language called "**desi**" was also spoken at the time; **D.C. Sarcar** considered it the shared base of Telugu and Kannad
*   **Universities at Dhanyakatakam and Nagarjunakonda** taught grammar, statecraft, economics, logic, mathematics, legal science, astrology and astronomy, drawing students from as far as abroad.

* * *

concepts.partName: Progress of Architecture, Sculpture and Painting
concepts.bodyMd:
### Architecture

*   Buddhism's growth filled the Deccan with **stupas, viharas and chaityas**. 

*   A **stupa** typically enshrined the remains of Buddha or Buddhist monks at its base, encircled by a cylindrical "methi" and capped with a half-dome; a **Pradakshina Patham** (circumambulation path) ran around it, with **Ayaka pillars, Prakaras and Toranas** at the entrances, and an umbrella-like **Harmika** crowning the whole structure. 
*   A **vihara** — the residence of monks and nuns, also called a Sangharama — was typically rectangular or square with a verandah and rooms on three sides fitted with stone sleeping benches; those with gardens for prayer and exercise were called "**Aramas**," and those used only during the rainy season, closer to towns, "**Varsharamas**." 
*   A **chaitya** served as the actual prayer hall — a spacious, pillared room.

*   The major stupas are at **Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda**. Others are found:
    
    *   In Andhra: Bhattiprolu, Ghantasala, Jaggayyapeta, Salihundam, Bavikonda, Totlakonda, Sankaram (Bojjannakonda), Goli, Anupu.
    *   In Telangana: Dhulikatta, Pasegam, Meerjampet (Karimnagar), Phanigiri (Nalgonda), Tirumalagiri.

*   The distinctive sculptural style of this period is known as **Amaravati art**, flourishing from the **2nd century B.C.E. to the 2nd century C.E.**, centered on Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda and Jaggayyapeta.
*   A recurring motif shows five pillars on each side of a platform, representing the **five stages of Buddha's life**:
    *   Lotus — birth
    *   Horse — Mahabhiniskramana (the Great Departure)
    *   Bodhi Tree — enlightenment
    *   Dharma Chakra — first sermon
    *   Stupa — parinirvana
*   Amaravati's influence travelled as far as **Southeast Asia** — Annam, Thailand, Java, Sumatra, Borneo.
*   **James Fergusson**, in his work _Tree and Serpent Worship_, ranked it as the highest achievement of the style.

*   Art critics attribute the colour paintings in **Ajanta cave numbers 9 and 10** (Aurangabad district, Maharashtra) to the Satavahana period, based on their stylistic closeness to Amaravati sculpture.
*   These depict scenes from **Mahayana Jataka stories**:
    *   Worship of the Bodhi Tree
    *   A dance by a group of fifteen figures
*   Similar period paintings survive in the cave temples of **Bedsa, Pithalkhora and Junnar**.

Once the Mauryan empire declined, the Satavahanas rose to independence and built a vast empire that endured for roughly **two and a half centuries**, from the 1st century B.C.E. to the 3rd century C.E. Starting from **Kotilingala**, their capital later moved to **Pratistanapura** and finally **Dhanyakatakam**, and the dynasty's most notable rulers — **Satakarni I, Gautamiputra Satakarni, Satakarni II, Vasishtiputra Pulumavi and Yagnasri Satakarni** — presided over a politically united and largely peaceful **Dakshinapatha**. 

Trade flourished, both internally and with Rome; towns and craft guilds prospered; and the Satavahanas proved themselves generous patrons of **Prakrit literature**. Religiously, the age saw Vedic tradition and **Buddhism** flourish side by side, Buddhism itself branching into numerous schools including Mahayana and Hinayana, and its influence shaping an entire school of art — Stupas, Chaityas and Viharas built on a scale unmatched before.

As the first dynasty to establish a truly extensive, stable, long-lasting empire in the Deccan — one that drove real economic and social development and left behind a lasting body of Prakrit and Sanskrit literature, architecture, sculpture and painting — the Satavahana age remains a genuinely **memorable chapter** in Indian history.
